QoL functions come a little too late for me to want to sit through the experience any further; if it were more like a visual novel, the experience would be significantly easier to digest and enjoy. As it is, 12 hours into the game, I find myself filling in the drudgery between bits of new dialogue with thoughts of how I really need to be doing something more productive.

candidates.text: 難易度very easyではありますが、1861年シナリオの南軍で勝利することができたので、自分が分かる限りのことをレビューさせていただきます。 まず、このゲームは知名度があまりありません。 日本においては皆無といって良いと思います。 当然日本語化MODもなければ日本語の情報もほとんどないです。 それでも、内容としてはこれ以上にないと思います。 南北戦争を描いたゲーム自体少ないかと思いますが、このゲームは細かいところまで精密に描写しています。 まず戦闘面においては、"ORDER DELAY"というシステムが搭載されています。 （設定でオフにすることもできます）軍隊は指揮官を通して命令を実行するわけですが、この時代には当然、電信はあっても無線機を兵士たちが所持している……なんてことはありません。 例えば軍団長が師団長に命令を発したとしたら、配下の人たちが馬に乗って師団長に命令を伝えに行きますし、師団長が各旅団長に命令を伝えるのにも、どうしても遅延が発生してしまいます。 部隊が遠くにいればその分命令を伝えるのに時間がかかってしまうので、できるだけ近くにいたほうがいい……といった感じです。 具体的には、"BUGLE RANGE"と"COMMAND RANGE"の二つがあります。 HQを中心に円状になっていて、BUGLE RANGEのなかにいればより早く命令が伝わりますし、より大きいサークルのCOMMAND RANGEのなかに居れば指揮官のボーナスが付与されます。 HQの位置が遠くて部隊に危機が迫っても中央司令部がすぐに対処することができない場合があったりすると、「自主的に対処してくれ……！ 」なんて思うことが多々あります。 個々の指揮官の自主性って大事なんだなあ。 別動隊を組織する場合は"AI STANCE"というのがあるので、これを設定しておくといい感じ。 例外ですが、自分のユニットを選択して敵ユニットを右クリックすると遅延なく攻撃することができます。 ビューグルとかドラム、手旗信号とかで攻撃命令を伝えてるのかな……。

candidates.title: Wingspan review
candidates.text: Wingspan is one of my favorite board games, if not my all-time favorite game. I don't think it's nearly as good as a digital experience and can't recommend it. This is an engine building game with very little interaction between players, and the loss of humans sitting at a table is too significant. The interface makes it difficult to keep track of what other players are even doing on their turns, so you're sort of left with your own board and no sense of how other players are doing on theirs, or even what birds they're playing. At my table, we always oooh and ahhhh over the birds as they are played and sometimes read the little trivia snippets to each other. In digital Wingspan it's hard to even know *when* another player is playing a bird since the interface does not naturally follow along with the actions of other players.Whether or not you're going to win feels like a crapshoot - and that's sort of how it is with tabletop Wingspan, but it's felt more keenly here since you won't be looking at the other boards very much, and you don't have anyone to talk to while you play.The automa mode is similarly diminished since, again, it's hard to follow along with how the automa is doing on its turns, so you're really just hoping you're doing better.Pretty disappointing! I'm not sure how this can be fixed. It just doesn't feel like a good fit for this medium.

It's fun trying to decide how to handle the challanges of the game as you try to find a base-layout that will satisfy the needs of the station and it's inhabitants. If you can see the pattern what I am saying is that Valheim is a repetitive mess. And the graphics don't help! --Overall Gameplay--You can try to make it enjoyable by moving around more, living in dangerous environments and doing creative challenges but the point is that the amount of content limits what you as the player can do. However, the main goal is to just get stacked build a base and defeat bosses. This can be a 'grindy' process for the casual player not to mention that this gets old fast when you realise that the environment is not lively at all and that there are no NPC's to meet (Other than the shop). This just makes the player feel like there is nothing else but their group of friends and that they won't come across something new. The abandoned villages are the only large structure on land and yet they are still extremely disappointing. They contain a couple chests beds and that's it. No story, no NPC's or some unique trait. The bosses are a great challenge and offer some really great opportunities to strategise but they are all still really easy to beat. --PvP--The first boss you encounter can be killed with just the first bow and a couple arrows and that's a BIG hint on what you are going to be coming across.

candidates.title: Valheim review
candidates.text: The game has its moments, like first taking off on a boat, appreciating your settlement after it's gotten to a certain size, fighting a troll for the first time... These things make the game enjoyable. Unfortunately, they are few and far between. What's occupying the rest of the time? Grinding resources--boar hides, copper, iron, etc. Once you start needing metal for all of your weapons, armor, tools, and upgrades, the game becomes a serious drag. You do almost nothing but search for new mining outcrops, crypts, etc. Even with a wagon, the process is unbearably slow and unfulfilling.The area you get iron from even seems designed to make people stop playing the game. I can understand making something challenging, but the challenges in this area are poisonous enemies, shuffling slowly through water as said enemies attack you, waiting for stamina to regenerate to raise more land, waiting for the right monster to spawn, creating new worlds specifically to farm more of these areas because they don't have enough buildings.The developers have included some cool features like deformable terrain, building structural integrity, and volumetric smoke/fog. The fighting is serviceable, but don't expect many surprises. I died to trees far more than I did to the bosses (never). When a group of small enemies provide more challenge and entertainment than a boss fight, it's not a good sign.If you have the masochism necessary to endure the grind, you will probably find many enjoyable moments in this game building cool settlements, fighting new monsters, and exploring new biomes. If you value your time, dislike spending the majority of your time mining, or appreciate a well thought-out world map, story, and occasionally having a conversation with an NPC, this game isn't for you.

candidates.title: Valheim review
candidates.text: I haven't felt this way about a video game since 2012 when my brother introduced me to a simple yet endlessly fun beta test game called Minecraft. Valheim is an incredible experience and everyone with an interest in survival, crafting, parry combat, vikings, or just casual fun gameplay should check it out. Graphics: ★★★★★-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Despite its low poly world design, Valheim does not look like a PS2 game. Somehow, through blooming and shadow detail and depth of field and a ton of other graphical enhancements, Valheim's relatively low-detail models look beautiful enough to make me forget that I'm even playing a video game. Gameplay: ★★★★★-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------I compare the gameplay to minecraft because my first night in Valheim felt so reminiscent of my first night in Minecraft, gathering basic materials, crafting primitive tools, and taking shelter in a hastily built home as night approached. I quickly discovered that combat in Valheim includes a rewarding block and parry system, as well as a dark souls style i-frame dodge mechanic. Blocking an enemy's projectile at the perfect moment will stun them, and offer enough time to roll forward and uppercut them with a fist, stab with a sword, or bash with a club. The combat system doesn't require high skill, but greatly rewards it. Story: ★★★★★-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Valheim's story acts as more of a framing device than a traditional narrative, and there are no cutscenes, dialogue, or voice acting. That being said, the game is best enjoyed cooperatively with multiple friends on the same world, and I loved making our own lore and story for the game. Valheim's world has a boss fight for each biome that will reward an item needed for the next biome to continue progression, and this progression loop is so satisfying.

candidates.text: I've played Valheim for over 3000 hours, and I can confidently say it is the best $20 I've ever spent! This game masterfully combines exploration and building, creating an experience that is both immersive and endlessly enjoyable.One of the standout features of Valheim is the balance it strikes between exploration and building. The biomes and scenery, while not boasting cutting-edge graphics, are beautifully crafted and create a captivating environment. Each biome feels distinct and offers unique challenges and resources, contributing to a sense of discovery and adventure.The game's development can sometimes feel slow, but the end results are always polished and satisfying. Each update brings new content and improvements that enhance the overall experience, demonstrating the developers' commitment to quality.Progression in Valheim is fun and challenging. It allows players to advance at their own pace without feeling pressured to rush. Whether you prefer tackling the game's challenges head-on or taking your time to build and explore, Valheim accommodates both playstyles beautifully.I've enjoyed the game both solo and with friends, playing with up to 8 players at once. The cooperative aspect is fantastic, and we've built some truly impressive structures together. From giant castles and sprawling towns to the great walls of the Plains and island fortresses, the building possibilities are virtually endless. There is so much to do if you have a builder's mindset, and the game provides ample tools and materials to let your creativity run wild.If I had to point out any weaknesses, it would be the lack of variation in the biomes. While each biome is beautifully crafted, more diversity would make exploration even more interesting and rewarding.

candidates.text: This is an okay game and it's nice to look at. There's some ideas in it that I like. candidates.title: Trials of Mana review
candidates.text: Trials of Mana is a cute and fun action RPG where you'll encounter puppies, bunnies, and pikachus... and beat the crap out of them for no good reason. Despite the childish visuals and story, the game has a deep class system that allows for plenty of creativity and customization. The game has some flaws, most of which don't apply if you just approach the game casually, but are quite annoying if you want to get more hardcore into the game.8/10Pros- The class system is really good. Each character has 4 different class paths they can take. With 6 total characters, this results in a lot of combinations and variety. There's a lot of replay value.- Combat, while simple, is fun and deeper than it initially seems. There's a lot of things to learn and a lot of things to be mindful of during combat.- Once you reach class 3, the game becomes incredibly fun. You get a lot of abilities that really open up what you can do in combat. After over 100 hours, I'm still having a blast trying out different combinations.- Graphics are cute and very good.- Angela is very sexy!Cons- AI is bad. They constantly get killed in boss fights (even in normal difficulty). They often just stand there instead of attacking enemies. They often sit on full resources without using abilities. They use random and useless abilities (player has zero control over which abilities they use). They don't do boss mechanics. They're slow to heal. While the game is easy enough that you can get through the game easily in hard difficulty and below, it's still hard to overlook such bad AI. AI needs to be better and the player really needs more settings to control AI behavior, such as enabling/disabling specific abilities.- Class 3 is where things really start to get fun with builds.

candidates.title: Dev Log: Combat System
candidates.text:
Hi engineers!

In the months following Dyson Sphere Program: Rise of the Dark Fog's showcase at TGS 2022, we received a lot of encouragement and support from our players. This has greatly motivated our team to put more effort into developing combat-related content. Let’s have a glance at the visuals we are currently working on:

During the combat system development, some optimization of existing gameplay systems was also introduced. Such as a new distribution logistics system, more advanced Chemical Plants, Splitters with storage, more convenient conveyor belt tools …

In order to maximize the team production effectiveness, we split our workflow into two branches - The Rise of the Dark Fog (combat system) branch and existing content updates. So that we can do these two parts of work at the same time, and keep the combat system info confidential. But we need to make sure to merge the changes made in the Update Branch into the Combat Branch from time to time, to ensure that the work on both sides is always in sync.

However, we also have a piece of bad news here: During the year that the combat system branch has been running separately, its content conflicts with the main branch have caused many code and resource issues. We had to put huge amounts of extra effort and time to resolve these problems every time, and sometimes we even have to deliberately avoid modifying common resources and low-level codes, which distracts us a lot from the combat system development. To speed up the progress of combat system development, we have decided to devote our full effort to the combat branch. In other words, we will still be able to debug and modify the existing game contents, but not be able to add any new features before the combat mode is grounding.

candidates.title: Warhammer 40,000: Darktide review
candidates.text: TLDR: Warhammer 40,000: Darktide is a fun and engaging game with great gameplay and atmosphere, but it is marred by an abundance of bugs and poorly implemented progression mechanics. The lack of a story and the release of the game before it was fully developed with missing mechanics are also major drawbacks. Fat Shark, the developer, has repeated the same mistakes from their previous games like Vermintide and Vermintide 2, which is disappointing.Regarding the gameplay, players and I have praised the game for its fast-paced and satisfying combat, as well as the variety of weapons and enemies available. The atmosphere of the game is also noteworthy, with a convincing portrayal of the grim and gritty Warhammer 40,000 universe.However, many players (which i am a part of) have reported a high number of bugs, such as crashes, glitches, and broken achievements. Some players have also experienced problems with the matchmaking system, making it difficult to find a stable game.The progression mechanics have also been criticized. For example, the lack of a clear leveling system makes it difficult to track character progress, and the gear system is confusing and not well-explained. Additionally, the game has a lack of story which is a major drawback for players who look for a good narrative experience.Lastly, the game has been criticized for being released too early, with many missing mechanics that are supposed to be included. This is particularly disappointing for fans of Fat Shark's previous games, Vermintide and Vermintide 2, as the developer seems to have repeated the same mistakes in terms of release timing and missing features.Overall, while Warhammer 40,000: Darktide has a lot of positive aspects, the game is flawed by a high number of bugs and poorly implemented progression mechanics, which detract from the overall experience.

candidates.title: OCTOPATH TRAVELER II review
candidates.text: Rating 8/10The music is good. The combat system is good. Building characters feels somewhat meaningful. The visuals are good, the game blurs things in the distance too much though. The character stories are all not bad. Some are better than others. My biggest disappointment with the game is that the characters do not interact with each other enough. candidates.title: Marvel's Midnight Suns review

If you're a marvel fan and are looking for a marvel game but don't like tactical combat, this game probably isn't for you. This isn't a real time action game and you must be able to accept that it's a turn based game.I will review every part of the game starting from what is best and ending with what is worst.Combat: 10 / 10 ; Hero Roster: 10 / 10 ; Game Audio: 10 / 10 ; Stable Gameplay 8 / 10: Attack Animations 8 / 10 ; Deck Building: 8 / 10 ; Writing 8 / 10 ; Balancing 7 / 10 ; Overall Graphics 6 / 10 ; Meta System: 7 / 10 ; Story: 6 / 10 ; Friendship System 6 / 10 ; Abbey Exploration 4 / 10It's important to understand there are five distinct parts of the game: Combat System, Story System (cutscenes and cinematics as well as idle conversations and optional character interactions), Meta System (deckbuilding / leveling up your heroes), Friendship System of building relationships with heroes (which ties directly into the Meta System) and Exploration System (Abbey Exploration). candidates.title: God of War review
candidates.text: And yet another example on why Steam needs to give us more options than "yes/no". God of War is a strange game, because as far as ports go, this is amazingly well done. A far cry from the dumpster-fire we were all anticipating from the jamokes at Sony Interactive. The thing about God of War is that it makes a great first impression. The presentation is rich, the combat functions without a hitch, and the overall world is overflowing with immense gravitas. In short, the game is well assembled. The art team, coders, modelers, etc all did their job and did them well.This is frustrating, because the core issue of the game really is just an endless parade of questionable design decisions. As many of you are aware, God of War tries for a new combat system that’s sort of akin to Dark Souls meets RE4. And RE4 is the comparison I find that I keep making, because the early issues with the game is that the game is extremely slow to dole out combat options. By the time I had the ability to do anything cool, I already had it ingrained in me to just safely stay back and continuously hucking axes until everything was dead, whether that was some green peon to a giant… uh…. Giant. Maybe I’d go into rage mode if I wanted to spice things up. And while it might be easy to simply say “well that’s your fault for playing like that”, the point is that the game (at least six hours in) does very little to incentivize you to utilize your full kit. Speaking of slow, pacing is also a rather irritating aspect of the game. Like many modern AAA, this one tries to go for a small, open world, seemingly for the sake of padding the runtime by forcing the player to backtrack (It’d be nice if the world was interesting enough to justify exploration for its own sake).

candidates.title: Warhammer 40,000: Darktide review
candidates.text: Darktide launched incomplete. I don't know why, but it was clearly not a finished game when it came out - from the lack of crafting, to the extremely limited skill trees, to the regular crashing and optimization issues, it was clear Darktide launched too soon, and it's overall rating reflects thatSo, a little over a year later, is it complete?At this point, it's probably as complete as Vermintide 1 was when it launched. So...no, it's not complete. But it IS whole. There's nothing significant that needs to be fixed or modified. It's incomplete in the sense that there's a lot more that's going to be added to the game from here on out. Or at least, that's what this developer's history would suggest to me. But we are at(or past) the point at which the game have launchedThere is a very solid core of fun gameplay here, built off the Vermintide system, but with significant changes to the ranged combat(both player and enemy). I wouldn't call Darktide's system an improvement on Vermintide's system so much as a pivot down a different direction.The melee gameplay is similar to Vermintide, which is to say, good. There are some differences(you can slide now - wheeee sliding), but for the most part the actual 'using weapons to bonk enemies' gameplay is unchangedThe ranged combat is in a good place. Ranged weapons are lethal, sound cool, and feel weighty.And the game great. All of the levels look good, the enemies are striking and memorable, the visuals on pretty much all the weapons are fantastic.The talents are well laid out, and none of the upgrade nodes really feel like insignificant upgrades.

candidates.title: OMORI review
candidates.text: This is another one of those situations where Steam really needs a "Neutral" or "Mixed" Review option. I enjoyed my time with this game overall, but it has some serious issues that makes me hesitant to recommend it at all.On the one hand, the last two hours or so is some of the most beautifully executed storytelling I've ever experienced. I have never had a game ending affect me so strongly emotionally the way Omori has.On the other hand, I found the gameplay to be sorely lacking and it absolutely killed the pacing at points. The battle system seems interesting at first, but it's only superficial and is lacking a lot of depth. Bosses have two or sometimes even one move they spam over and over with no variation and normal encounters feel borderline pointless.Even outside of the boring combat, most NPC interactions and 'puzzles' feel like chores and are quirky for the sake of being quirky. There are plenty of good moments and the writing and characterisation is solid throughout, especially in the non-headspace parts of the game, but these moments are broken up by hours of tedium and boredom.If you don't mind wallowing through about 15-20 hours of shallow, forgettable filler then there's a great story here that I'd say is worth experiencing. candidates.text: I love the concepts behind this game - but in many cases I find the actual implementation of these concepts lacking.What I liked:* The main premise of the game - the fact that characters change and evolve over time, in response to both combat and non-combat events - is definitely cool. And many of these changes have interesting combat implications.* I love how mages work in this game - it's novel, interesting, and adds a lot of interactivity to the combat arenas.* I love how in-combat death is handled! And it's actually a deeper system than it appears at first, with aspects like one character sacrificing themslves for another, permanent maiming, building graves for fallen characters, and more.* Catching spirits is fun :-)What I didn't like:* My number 1 complaint is that I find the dialogs tedious. Extremely tedious. They play a large and important role in this game - they are not just filler between combat missions - and they are often too long, too unclear, and in many cases, too vague and philosophical. It got to a point where I just wanted to skip them, which for this kind of game is a sign that I should probably stop playing.* And in addition, for me, the dialogs didn't really convey consistent character personality; and I didn't perceive any consistent character relationship with the exception of the explicit relationships you pick, which are few in number.* The combat difficulty progresses weirdly. I'd say a majority of the encounters were too easy, a small number extremely hard, and only for a small minority I felt they were truly challenging but fair. Plus character progression significantly increases the power of each character, which means that new recruits typically provide relatively little value when added at a later chapter, making the difficulty curve even wonkier - encounters become cakewalk with too many veterans and impossible with too many newbies.* There are only 3 classes.

candidates.title: Hades review

The thing that I don't like about the progression system is that it is build around playing the game to gather resources to make yourself permanently stronger. So you get farther every run, but not necessarily because you get better at the game, but because you made the game easier. candidates.title: DevBlog #2: New Unit System.
candidates.text:
This is the 2nd blog in our new series, which discusses developing our updated engine that will power the next title in the Grand Tactician-series. We're keeping some details, like historical setting, vague on purpose to discuss at a later stage. But, we’ll keep releasing these peeks behind the scenes to let you know what to expect in terms of game play and improvements.

The New Unit System

One of the first things we developed for The Civil War (during 2016-17) was what we call the Unit System. This is how units are created and handled in the battle layer, and it has a big impact on a multitude of other things: visuals, controls, performance, AI, to name a few.

Re-building the Unit System is a key part of improving the battle layer for the upcoming title. The results are very encouraging and we’re excited about the possibilities it brings to the table, both for game play and also for performance and clunkiness (or lack of, this time around) of the battles. This will of course work hand-in-hand with terrain and movement, group-system, combat system(s), AI, and so on.

The Old System

In the old system, we built the units from what we call “company blocks”. These are sub-elements of the units, and platforms, that are moved depending on the unit’s formation and positioning. The 3D models (or as the game originally featured, sprite soldiers!) are attached to each platform.

candidates.title: Black Myth: Wukong review
candidates.text: The graphics are stunning, and the map looks great. However, the map design itself is a complete mess, cluttered and lacking in distinctiveness. Coupled with the numerous and unreasonable invisible walls, it's hard not to think that this is all just for the sake of the visuals and art—a case of style over substance.The boss design feels uneven. Some monsters are satisfying to fight against, while others are just plain annoying. Either their hit boxes are weird, or the bosses have irritating moves. In soul-like games, they are tough, but you can find tricks and rhythms to gradually conquer them. However, the bosses in this game seem to rely on luck: the hit boxes are terrible, I dodge but somehow still get hit by the boss. There are various unreasonable jumping slashes and attack patterns that feel like they're locked in. Then there's the stitched-together combat system: the protagonist has a mana bar, extremely long cooldowns for skills, a stamina bar, perfect dodge, charge attacks, non-cancellable heavy attacks, very slow light attacks, and no defense... Fighting bosses feels like it's just for the sake of progressing through the game, most of them aren't enjoyable.The mana bar and extremely long cooldowns make it frustrating when you misuse a spell; the stamina bar means you have to rest a bit after a combo when fighting bosses; the very slow basic attacks (both light and heavy, plus the charge bar) don't give you the exhilarating, mindless slashing satisfaction found in games like God of War because there's no defense, and you constantly have to watch out for running out of energy and sudden counterattacks from enemies. The whole combat system feels pieced together and lacks a cohesive system.

candidates.title: February Content Update
candidates.text:
We're very aware that we've been creeping up in performance requirements lately and so this update we did a bit of spring cleaning early! We've boosted FPS and lowered CPU usage across the board by optimization in dialog cameras, NPCs roaming around the world, textures, particles and more!

We're always working on continually improving the performance in the game and we're currently prototyping some much more radical changes.

Combat

We've changed our targeting system, moving back to our previous system with dynamic targeting. We felt that managing two combat targeting systems(which is what we had) ended up being messy and not what we intended; now we're focusing on polishing and making one system. Additionally, a change some of you will notice is that thrust attack is now sprint + regular attack rather than having it's own keybind.

We're currently working on incorporating magic into the combat system this will be coming later this year with it's own quest. Ranged upgrades and improvements are also on the way with bow crafting, arrows and some changes to enemy behavior.

Squish goes the Bug

We've tried our best to go through as many bugs we could find in the update and fix as many as we can in time for the update, including issues with Milk and Honey, Quest tracking, day/night issues, fast travel, NPCs, animations, typos, save/load issues and more! On / after the previous 0.3.0 update & 0.3.1 hotfix (which was around 4-5 months ago as of writing this), developers have stated that they'll be releasing fewer but bigger updates, which I'm entirely cool with. Seeing a new update, and how the developers stating that this is the biggest one yet, I was hoping to see new hull types, tools, tool upgrades, etc... content so to speak. The 0.4.0 update; the biggest update yet did nothing on these three main things I consider content in this game, unfortunately. There is a new ship type in the said update, and more variations on ships, but these don't add much for me; they still use the same ship hulls, and there's just three hull types. candidates.text: I had been somewhat dreading my own experience with this game because I had seen the advertisements and early reviews claiming how different Frostpunk 2 is to the first game. And while this is true, the real question is if these changes are for the better? I'd say its pretty subjective.In terms of tone, Frostpunk 2 is very different from its predecessor. In the first game, there was this constant eldritch horror of being at the mercy of the elements, with several hundred survivors huddled around a generator, building to distract themselves from the reality of 90% of humanity being wiped out by an apocalyptic natural disaster. In the sequel, this tone has been replaced with a dreadful sense of never ending tension and feeling constantly short-handed by the various factions and preventing them (and yourself, Steward) from going to extremes too quickly. And this is understandable because the scope of the game is bigger and you have multiple settlements and colonies to manage on top of your main city. If Frostpunk 1 was about several hundred survivors trying to build a post-apocalyptic community, Frostpunk 2 is about managing several communities to build the foundation of a post-apocalyptic nation.The social management aspect of Frostpunk 2 is where most of the action in the game lies, which probably explains why the economic systems of this game remain relatively simple (and time management honestly matters less compared to the first game). It is the constant tension between factions that will drain your heatstamps and drain your resources more than any natural disaster in Frostpunk 2. And this is probably what makes the learning curve of Frostpunk 2 harder than its predecessor because even at the lowest difficulty, things can fall apart very quickly unless you want to turn into a dictator or just favour one faction from the get go.I really want to like this game, I do appreciate the thought and care put into building on the foundations of the first game to create something new.

candidates.title: Frostpunk 2 review
candidates.text: Frostpunk 2 is a good game and worth buying, but there are a lot of pros and cons to it. The community seems divided over it being both too similar, and too different from Frostpunk 1 at the same time. FP2 is same in the ways it functions, you place buildings, get resources, and make crucial decisions to quell unrest. Its also the same, if not better, in terms of atmosphere. The sound and graphic design are really good, city wide announcements like "Citizens, please make way for frostbreaking teams in transit" add a surprising amount of satisfaction in ambience, and the music is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ unbelievably good, much like the first game.The problem arises with the scale of FP2. The magic of FP1 was racing against the clock, knowing your small settlement had to absolutely haul ass in order to survive -200C storms. Every. Decision. Mattered. This game has that to a degree, but not nearly as much. Resources are more complicated, the UI is not as easy to read, and the city is more zoomed out, with reduced intimacy with your citizens. It is overall harder to understand how much your citizens are fighting for survival, how successful you are managing things, and is less satisfying when you pull off a difficult maneuver.This makes absolute sense logically, the city is massive after all. But is it worth it? If you want the experience of Frostpunk, but haven't played the first game, I recommend getting FP1. Its one of the best games ever made imo. But if you've played FP1, this is an excellent successor with a lot of heart put into it. Unfortunately the devs had the near impossible task of making a sequel to what was essentially a perfect game. That being said, in the 6 years since FP1, I would've really liked to see more large gameplay mechanics added.

candidates.title: Frostpunk 2 review
candidates.text: Frostpunk 2 is an excellent evolution of the first game through both gameplay and themes while retaining the core ideas that made the original special.Gameplay:This is still your gruelingly difficult steampunk cold fighting city builder game - but at a level higher than in the previous game. Instead of micro-managing a workforce of a few hundred, you are in charge of thousands organizing workforces of hundreds through districts. Furthermore, you can expand the interests of New London to new locations. The game has a clear influence on some of the mechanics introduced in the "On the Edge" DLC from the first game. Logistics is everything. Ensure there is enough housing. Ensure your new districts dont overwhelm your heat demand. Ensure your new population is fed. Ensure your buildings are being maintained.Along with this, the tech tree is now split on ideas by the factions you will encounter. Each have some interesting benefits or setbacks that have their appeal. Some techs will require a law to be introduced and passed by the council.The council is able to pass laws that attend to issues in the city, though you do not have the same authority as in the first game. A bill can be proposed as a law, and depending on the different delegates' worldviews, it will or wont go through. Some of the laws that need to be researched first can be a bit out of the way, or rarely encountered and is one of the main criticisms I have for this mechanic.I find it hard to believe that it takes about the same amount of time for my researchers to understand machinery used to recycle heat as it does the idea for privatized alcohol.Sound Design and Music:Much of the appeal of the first game comes from its presentation in sound and music, and that carries over the the second game. The light groaning of the generator in the first game has been replaced by intimidating sounds of machinery that echoes through the much larger city.

candidates.title: Frostpunk 2 review
candidates.text: Frostpunk 2 is not - shocker - Frostpunk 1. It's a progression; a 'what if' wherein 30 years have passed since the first game and now it's time to try to do more than just hide from the ice in a hole. That hole isn't big enough anymore; there are thousands of people and more every day, and despite the storms coming in and wrecking everything exposed over and over, there literally isn't room to keep everyone in that little hole, and decisions have to be made.That's what Frostpunk 2 is about, in in many ways what it does share with the first game: decisions. In many ways I even feel it does decisions , because unlike the first game I have yet to find a situation where there is one best path that will see you through on the harder difficulties. In FP1, above certain difficulties you played a certain way or you lost. FP2, with its factional clashing preventing you from treading the exact path you planned, that isn't ven possible.The game is still beautiful - although I did find more visual impressiveness in the first. I hope desperately they at least add screenshot modes to 2 the way they did the first game.The narrative takes place at a bit more of a remove because, again, thousands of people rather than tens and hundreds. Interestingly though, I actually feel more immersed. In Frostpunk 1, the Captain was a nebulous individual who nudged the ant colony along particular lines. In 2... I'm a harried leader who people actually come to with demands, and who I have to bend to my intentions if I want to get anywhere. Do I want to use the moss-based air scrubbers because they work better and I only have so much space in my residential districts?

candidates.title: Age of Empires III: Definitive Edition review
candidates.text: Age of Empires III: Definitive Edition was supposed to be a grand return to form, a polished update of a classic RTS that once stood tall among its peers. But let’s be honest: it’s a bit of a letdown. Released in 2020, this "Definitive Edition" feels anything but. Instead of being a celebration of what made the original great, it’s more like a sluggish, clunky rehash that struggles to justify its existence in today's gaming landscape.First off, let’s talk about the graphics. It’s 2020 (well, 2024 now), and this game looks like it’s stuck in the early 2010s. Sure, the devs slapped on some new textures and called it a day, but honestly, it’s not enough. The visuals are inconsistent, with some units and buildings looking okay-ish, while others are painfully outdated. The environments, which should be immersive and detailed, instead feel flat and lifeless. For a game that's supposed to be definitive, it’s disappointing that it doesn't even look as good as some modern indie RTS games. It might have looked fine back in the day, but now it’s just plain underwhelming.Then there’s the gameplay. Age of Empires III always had its quirks, but those quirks now feel more like flaws in this definitive edition. The gameplay is clunky, and the controls feel unresponsive at times. Units sometimes don’t do what you tell them to, and managing large groups of them is more frustrating than it should be. Pathfinding issues that were a pain in the original still persist here, making you wonder what they actually improved in this edition.The pacing of the game is another issue. It’s slow. Like, painfully slow.

candidates.title: Age of Empires III: Definitive Edition review
candidates.text: Pathfinding issues that were a pain in the original still persist here, making you wonder what they actually improved in this edition.The pacing of the game is another issue. It’s slow. Like, painfully slow. In a genre where games like StarCraft II and even Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition manage to keep things engaging, Age of Empires III: DE feels like it’s dragging its feet. The AI isn't particularly challenging either, which makes single-player matches more of a slog than a strategic battle of wits.Okay, so what about the new content? They added some new civilizations and game modes, but it honestly feels like a thin layer of frosting on a stale cake. The new civs don’t do much to shake up the formula, and the historical battles are more of a chore than an exciting addition. It’s clear the developers tried to add some value, but these additions feel tacked on and don’t really address the underlying issues with the game.Multiplayer could’ve been this game’s saving grace, but nope, it’s just as frustrating. The matchmaking is slow, and there are still a bunch of bugs that can ruin matches. Lag spikes and disconnects are more common than they should be in a game that’s supposed to be a polished, definitive experience. And good luck trying to find a decently balanced match—half the time you’re either steamrolling or getting steamrolled.At the end of the day, Age of Empires III: Definitive Edition is a boring, clunky mess that doesn’t live up to its promise. It looks like it belongs in the past, and not in a nostalgic way, but in a “wow, games used to be this rough?” kind of way.

candidates.text: I have been a fan of this game since it was released in 2007.... I have never written a Steam review.I pre-purchased this game and counted down the days to play it with 4 friends doing the same.First game I played with 2 other long time players in multiplayer. So we know the game inside out...First impressions - graphics are muddy and inconsistent, sounds is the same or worse.Better intro.. but would assume so its 13 years later...The first time playing multiplayer the game was jerky and laggy. I guess because most long time players would have them unlocked in the old one?The explorer has a giant halo around him?The hotkeys - while can be changed are different from the original. Why?After 1 game myself and friends opted to play the old one, while waiting for this game why all payed money for to be fixed. Waited for the day 1 hotfix.Played second game, slightly improved, still experienced stutter then CRASHED after 40 mins of playing together; all players booted to windows.Why did I pay for this game? candidates.title: Age of Empires III: Definitive Edition review
candidates.text: A hot and steaming pile of S**T.Being an OG player since around the time AOE2 came out, you bet your bottom dollar I was ripping AOE3 off of BitTorrent the moment the trial was released. And then drooling over the new expansions at my local Game Stop some years later. Having played thousands of matches and hundreds of hours this has been one of my favorites of all time.However, I couldn't believe what I saw when I purchased this Definitive Edition. From clunky UI, to ugly graphics, to new sounds and icons that were completely undue for a change, they have taken all the nostalgia right out of this game for me. The game plays so different from the original, at one point I had thought I accidentally bought AOE4 or something. Overall, the look of graphics is less realistic and more simplified, and some of the new buttons don't look like they belong in this game at all. It's like a dev played Fortnite for 20 hrs straight, then sat down to reskin our beloved franchise.The new added UI is organized way differently than the original but with no purpose in mind. It blocks key parts of the screen (especially the bottom left), making it hard to see units. On top of that, there's weird new numbers next to everything. New animations, sounds, and icons have been added to each unit. Why? What was wrong with the originals? The buildings too have been re-textured, but the scaling is so small and so poorly done that the 14-year-old graphics of 2007 AOE3 still out-do these modern ones by a long shot.
